content: Dead-in-bed syndrome refers to the sudden and unexpected death of young individuals with type 1 diabetes who have no prior history of diabetic complications, particularly autonomic dysfunction. These individuals are typically found deceased in an undisturbed bed, which suggests that death did not occur during a convulsive episode. This phenomenon was first described in 1991 in a study involving 20 patients. The proposed causes of dead-in-bed syndrome include the following: 1. Hypoglycemic unawareness, also known as the hypoglycemia-unawareness syndrome, where individuals fail to recognize the symptoms of low blood sugar. 2. Ventricular dysrhythmias induced by hypoglycemia, which may occur due to QT interval prolongation during episodes of low blood sugar. 3. Autonomic dysfunction triggered by hypoglycemia, which can also result in ventricular dysrhythmias due to QT prolongation. For diagnostic purposes, diabetic ketoacidosis can be investigated post-mortem by analyzing the biochemical composition of vitreous fluid obtained during an autopsy. Preventing nocturnal hypoglycemia is a key strategy to reduce the risk of dead-in-bed syndrome. Continuous glucose monitoring systems can help detect and prevent episodes of low blood sugar during sleep. The American Diabetes Association's clinical practice guidelines suggest that the MiniMed® Paradigm™ Veo system may be one of the most effective tools for this purpose, although its cost-effectiveness remains uncertain. Closed-loop systems, often referred to as artificial pancreases, have also shown promise in preventing hypoglycemia according to systematic reviews. However, it is important to note that even with the use of glucose sensors, the complete prevention of dead-in-bed syndrome cannot be guaranteed.
